title: Red, Green, Refactor
summary: A failing test for a new rule, the smallest change that passes it, then a cleanup pass the tests protect.
signals: production changes with no test in the same commit
a big feature implemented in one pass, tests written afterward to match it
a bugfix with no new test pinning the bug
hesitation to clean up code because "it works, don't touch it"

roles.Order: the module under test, at a snapshot in its TDD cycle
roles.cancel(): the operation the new rule constrains
roles.a shipped order can't be cancelled: the new requirement driving the cycle
roles.the red test: the new assertion, written before the code satisfies it
roles.the guard: the minimal production change that makes the red test pass
roles.canCancel(): the refactor: the same rule, named and pulled out of cancel(), behind the same public shape as green

stages.title: Red
stages.idea: The new rule doesn't exist yet. The test that will drive it currently documents the flaw it will fix.

stages.title: Green
stages.idea: The smallest change that satisfies the new rule — deliberately crude, a bare status comparison.

stages.title: Refactor
stages.idea: Same behaviour, cleaner design: the rule gets a name. The same tests prove nothing broke.

checks: Why does the red stage's test assert the current, flawed behaviour instead of being marked failing or skipped?
What makes the green stage's fix "deliberately crude", and why is that acceptable at that point?
What must stay identical between the green and refactor stages, and what proves it?
Why is skipping the refactor step not "saving time"?
